summary: Defines extra L2TPv3 bit values in the Circuit Status AVP to report finer-grained error states for attachment circuits and pseudowires. It also generalizes the Active bit and deprecates the use of the New bit in the Circuit Status AVP.

plainLanguage.summary: A traffic light with only green and red isn't enough. This adds more colors so an L2TPv3 link can say exactly what is wrong.

questions: what is the l2tpv3 circuit status avp
what does the n bit mean in l2tpv3
what are l2tpv3 fault status bits
subtitle: Seven status bits let an L2TPv3 endpoint say which direction of a link has failed, and whether a pseudowire is on standby.

tldr.problem: The L2TPv3 Circuit Status AVP could only say that a circuit was up or down. That does not show which direction failed, and it cannot show that a pseudowire is held in reserve.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5641 adds five bit values to the Circuit Status AVP: four fault bits (R, T, I, E) and a Standby bit (S). It also redefines the Active bit as 'no faults on the local pseudowire endpoint' and deprecates the New bit.
tldr.outcome: Old and new implementations can still interwork, because the Active bit stays set only when no fault bit is set. The RFC updates RFC 3931, RFC 4349, RFC 4454, RFC 4591 and RFC 4719.

facts.label: New bits
facts.value: Bits 9 through 13 (S, E, I, T, R)

today: RFC 5641 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3931, RFC 4349, RFC 4454, RFC 4591 and RFC 4719.

sections.title: Why a Finer Status Is Needed
sections.content:
L2TPv3 carries layer 2 traffic, such as Frame Relay or Ethernet, across a packet network. Each carried circuit is bound to a session, and the Circuit Status AVP from RFC 3931 tells the peer whether that circuit is up or down.

Up or down is often too coarse. A finer granularity helps find the direction of a fault, as was already added for MPLS-based pseudowires that use the Label Distribution Protocol (see RFC 4446 and RFC 4447). It is also useful, in session-level redundancy setups, to mark a pseudowire as standby: fully signaled and open to Operations, Administration, and Maintenance, but not switching data.

The new bits are added in a backwards compatible way and apply to every pseudowire type that uses the Circuit Status AVP.
sections.plainLanguage: A plain on/off light cannot tell you what is wrong. This RFC adds more lights so the two ends of a link can say what is broken and which way.

sections.title: The Circuit Status AVP Value
sections.content:
The Circuit Status AVP is Attribute Type 71. It can appear in ICRQ, ICRP, ICCN, OCRQ, OCRP, OCCN and SLI messages, and it gives the initial status of the circuit bound to a session, or a status change.

Its value is a 16-bit field. Before this RFC only two bits were defined: A (Active, bit 15, 0x0001) and N (New, bit 14, 0x0002). RFC 5641 keeps them and adds five more, giving the layout Reserved | S | E | I | T | R | N | A.

Bit numbering counts from the left of the 16-bit field, so the Active bit is bit 15 and the Standby bit is bit 9.
sections.plainLanguage: The status is a row of 16 little switches. Two used to mean something. Now seven do, and the rest are saved for later.

sections.title: The New Fault and Standby Bits
sections.content:
The four fault status bits describe the local pseudowire endpoint, which covers the local Attachment Circuit (AC) and the endpoint that faces the packet switched network (PSN).

  • R: the AC cannot receive traffic, but can still transmit.
  • T: the AC cannot transmit traffic, but can still receive.
  • I: a fault in the receive direction between the local endpoint and the remote L2TP endpoint.
  • E: a fault in the transmit direction between the local endpoint and the remote L2TP endpoint.

For I and E, the RFC notes that a session-level fault would not necessarily cause an L2TP control connection timeout. How the fault is detected is out of scope; examples given are PW Type-specific means and Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD).

The S bit means the pseudowire is in Standby mode. It was signaled during setup and is operational, but it is NOT switching user traffic. Received user traffic SHOULD be dropped, and user traffic MUST NOT be transmitted. A standby pseudowire can still have its data plane liveness checked, for example as in RFC 5085.
sections.plainLanguage: Four of the switches say 'I can't hear' or 'I can't talk' for two different parts of the path. The fifth says 'I'm on the bench: ready to play, but not playing right now.'

sections.title: Rules for Setting the Bits
sections.content:
Older implementations set bits 0 to 13 to zero, so they can interwork with new ones. The RFC then gives these rules:

  • If several faults occur, every matching fault bit MUST be set (bitwise OR).
  • The A bit MUST NOT be set until all fault bits are cleared, and if any fault bit is set, A MUST be cleared. This lets an endpoint work with a remote endpoint that does not understand the new bits.
  • If A and all fault bits are clear, there is no extended status. The circuit is simply down.
  • S can be set together with any other bit, including A. Leaving standby is shown by clearing S.

The A bit is redefined. RFC 3931 tied it to the local access circuit only. Now it means that no faults are present on the local pseudowire endpoint.

The N bit, which says whether a notification is for a new or an existing circuit, is deprecated. It SHOULD be ignored on receipt and is OPTIONAL to set on sending, because the control message type already tells the receiver most of what it conveys.
sections.plainLanguage: If anything is wrong, the 'all good' switch must be off. If nothing is wrong, it must be on. That way, an older device that only knows 'good or bad' still understands.

sections.title: Changes to Existing RFCs
sections.content:
The Active and New bits were first defined in Section 5.4.5 of RFC 3931 and were repeated for specific circuit types. RFC 5641 updates the definitions in five documents: RFC 3931, RFC 4349 (HDLC), RFC 4454 (ATM), RFC 4591 (Frame Relay) and RFC 4719 (Ethernet).

It also removes two sentences from Section 2.2 of RFC 4719 that required the New bit to be set for ICRQ and ICRP and cleared for ICCN and SLI. In four of the documents it adds a paragraph saying that, since the N bit is deprecated, the sender need not indicate it and the receiver need not check it.
sections.plainLanguage: When you change a rule in one rulebook, you have to fix the copies in the other rulebooks too. This RFC lists which pages to fix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds nothing new here. Security considerations for the Circuit Status AVP are covered in Section 8 of RFC 3931, and the RFC states that no additional security considerations exist from extending the attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding more switches does not add new ways to break in, so the old safety rules still apply.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The Circuit Status Bits number space is managed by IANA under Section 10.7 of RFC 3931. Five new bits, 9 through 13, and one updated bit, 14, were assigned. Bit 9 is S, 10 is E, 11 is I, 12 is T, 13 is R, and bit 14 is N, marked as use deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list keeps track of what each switch means, so everyone agrees. These new switches were added to it.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Bits 0 to 8; unused and set to zero.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Bit 9: pseudowire is in Standby mode.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Bit 10: local PSN-facing PW egress transmit fault.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Bit 11: local PSN-facing PW ingress receive fault.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Bit 12: local AC egress transmit fault.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Bit 13: local AC ingress receive fault.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Bit 15: Active; no faults on the local pseudowire endpoint.
